newsitem.title: USA: US House panel approves stock decimalization bill.
newsitem.headline: US House panel approves stock decimalization bill.

text.p: A House panel on Wednesday approved a measure that would allow stocks on U.S. exchanges to trade in smaller increments by requiring them to be traded in decimals rather than in fractions.

The bill, which calls on the Securities and Exchange Commission to develop a plan within a year to move stock and options markets away from trading in fractions, was passed on a voice vote by the finance subcommittee of the House Commerce Committee.

"Fractional pricing, whether in intervals of an eighth, a sixteenth, or even small fractions ... still imposes an artificial limit on investors' ability to get better prices through competition," said subcommittee chairman Michael Oxley, an Ohio Republican.
Members of the panel from New York all opposed the measure. They included ranking Democrat Thomas Manton, Republican Rick Lazio and Democrat Eliot Engel.
"I remain unconvinced that our system needs to be fixed," Manton said, echoing the concerns of the securities industry.
All of the New York members said such a move should be made by the market and not mandated by Congress.
Most stocks are traded in eighths or sixteenths of a dollar, so the smallest trading increment is either 12.5 cents or 6.25 cents, respectively.
Switching to decimals, could, in theory, allow these spreads to shrink to as little as one cent.

Separately the panel approved a bill that sets funding for the SEC at $320 million for fiscal 1998 and $342.7 million for 1999. Those funding levels were the amounts the SEC sought in its budget request.
